Jane Street ASIC puzzle · A reverse-engineering writeup

How to reverse engineer an ASIC without understanding the circuit

Recover the wiring. Make the circuit executable. Then search what it can say.

I’m a computer science student, not a hardware engineer. Before this puzzle, most of my hardware experience was with Verilog.

I started by reading the problem statement closely:

We’ve designed an ASIC, and we’re giving you its final mask: all of its metal, routing, and active transistor layers, along with some sample inputs and outputs.

Your job is to reverse engineer it. First, recover a netlist from the layout. Then figure out the circuit’s true purpose. And then comes the puzzle within the puzzle: once you understand what the chip does, use it to tease out the output it’s looking for, and find the string value that’s your final answer.

The repository included the puzzle files and a warm-up showing the complete design flow from Verilog to GDS, the final physical layout:

asic-puzzle-2026/
├── puzzle.gds                         ← reverse this
├── example_inputs.vcd                 ← sample inputs and outputs
└── warmup/
    ├── 00_source.v                    ← original Verilog
    ├── 01_netlist.v                   ← target representation
    ├── 02_netlist_with_power_rails.v
    ├── 03_post_place_and_route.def
    └── 04_final.gds                   ← final layout

To see what the GDS files contained, I opened them in the TinyTapeout GDS Viewer.

And hey, what do you know? It was the same viewer used for the image at the top of the puzzle’s blog post.

More usefully, the viewer showed that the GDS preserved both the physical layers and the standard-cell instances—the individual building blocks of the circuit. Their names identified them as members of SkyWater’s SKY130 standard-cell library.

That gave me a starting point. I could identify the cells from their library definitions, then reconstruct their connections from the layout.

Extracting the circuit

I used KLayout’s Python API to extract the standard cells and their connections.

The extraction followed the physical wiring. KLayout merged touching conductor shapes within each layer, connected layers through contacts and vias, and assigned each connected component a net ID. Pins reached by the same connected component belonged to the same net.

I then matched the extracted cells against the SKY130 definitions to identify their pins, input and output directions, and logical behavior.

For each extracted instance, I recorded its cell type and the direction and net ID of every connected pin. The physical layout had become a netlist: a description of the circuit’s components and how they were wired together.

Simulating the recovered circuit

The extracted data now described the logical circuit:

  • Cell types, which identified the logic performed by each standard cell.
  • Pins and directions, which identified the inputs and outputs of each cell.
  • Net IDs, which connected output pins to the input pins they supplied.

The SKY130 library also provided the Verilog models needed to simulate those cells.

For this logical simulation, I filtered out the power rails and cells used only for power connections.

The remaining data mapped almost directly to structural Verilog:

  • Each signal net became a wire.
  • Each cell type selected the corresponding SKY130 module.
  • Each cell instance became a module instance.
  • Each pin became a named module argument connected to the wire with the same net ID.

I wrote a generator that applied this mapping and recovered the module's top-level ports from the named nets at the edge of the layout.

I compiled the generated Verilog with Icarus Verilog and ran the warm-up. Its behavior was consistent with the known circuit—a promising first check that the extraction worked.

Checking the connections

Simulation let me run the circuit, but a long Verilog file was still awkward to inspect.

I converted the netlist into a NetworkX graph and plotted it with Matplotlib, showing the logical cells, nets, top-level ports, and connections.

The warm-up gave me a direct comparison: I could build one graph from the supplied netlist and another from my reconstruction.

NetworkX found that the two graphs were isomorphic: they had the same connection structure. The reconstruction had recovered the warm-up’s wiring.

Inspecting the puzzle

With that check in place, I applied the same graph-building code to the puzzle. Its reconstructed graph contained 738 logical cells and 717 electrical nets.

The circuit was executable, and I could see all its connections. What I still could not see was its purpose.

I first tried dividing the graph into communities of closely connected cells, hoping they would correspond to recognizable parts of the design. They did not. Even on the warm-up, the communities mixed logic from different source blocks. A later experiment with DANA grouped related flip-flops, but still did not explain the puzzle.

To go further, I needed a representation I could manipulate as well as run. I generated a Python version of the circuit.

That required making the execution order explicit:

  • The combinational logic had to be topologically sorted so that no instruction ran before the values it needed had been calculated.
  • The flip-flops became state variables and were updated separately from the combinational logic.

Boolean collapse

My first approach was to combine the individual gates into larger Boolean expressions.

For each cell, I recursively substituted its expression wherever another cell used its output. I then passed the expanded expressions to SymPy’s simplify_logic, hoping that simplification would reveal a recognizable rule.

On the warm-up, it did. The simplified success expression had fifteen terms involving two 8-bit input registers, A and B. Each term specified one accepted pair.

A bit written directly had to be 1; a negated bit had to be 0. Reading those requirements as numbers revealed the same rule in every term, A + B = 496.

Inspect the full collapse, all 15 terms and accepted pairs

The terms are joined by OR. Within each row, all bit requirements are joined by AND. Register bits are shown from 0 to 7, least significant first.

Replace each literal with its required bit value.

Converting each register to decimal gives these fifteen pairs.

The warm-up source raised success when A + B = 496. The collapsed expression had recovered that original condition.

I tried the same approach on the puzzle. This time, the expressions grew enormously without revealing a comparable rule. Combining the gates had made the formulas larger, but had not made the circuit easier to understand.

Asking the circuit precise questions

Instead of trying to explain the entire circuit, I asked a smaller question:

Given the bytes it had already emitted, what byte could come next?

There were 2121 possible inputs, but only 256 possible values for the next output byte. I could search the outputs and ask Z3, a constraint solver, to find inputs that produced them.

I modeled the testbench in Z3, with each cycle’s resulting state feeding the next. The input bits stayed symbolic, so Z3 could choose their values to satisfy the output I requested.

I could then constrain the output and ask whether any input satisfied the complete model. Z3 returned SAT if such an input existed and UNSAT if none did.

Finding one byte was not enough. Starting with an empty output prefix, I excluded each byte Z3 returned and asked again. Only an UNSAT result established that no continuation remained.

I repeated this process for each continuation, extending the prefix one byte at a time. A zero byte ended a message. The result was a tree of every possible output message, built without first identifying the computation behind it.

Eventually, the tree stopped growing. Under the modeled input and readout sequence, the circuit could emit exactly five messages across all possible 121-bit inputs.

For each message, Z3 also supplied a concrete input that produced it.

I later learned that this was a Star Battle board. To show the inputs in that form, I’ve arranged each 121-bit sequence into eleven rows of eleven, with the original serial sequence beneath it.

Five messages, one successful input

Only the last of these inputs raised success.

To check it outside Z3, I reset the ordinary Python circuit evaluator and replayed the 121 bits in their original serial order. It emitted (* TWO STARS *) and raised success again.

That was the answer. I had recovered enough of the circuit to reproduce its behavior, then searched that behavior to find the successful input. Understanding the purpose of every group of gates had never become necessary.

Postscript: searching by circuit activation

After solving the puzzle, I tried a different approach: could a learned search discover interesting boards by activating parts of the circuit that earlier boards had not reached?

The idea was to supply a board, record which internal values became true, and search for edits that activated something new.

I traced backward from the output bus to identify internal values that could affect the output. For each board, the Python evaluator recorded which of those values became true during the input and readout cycles. The same value at two different clocks counted as two separate coverage items.

Combining those records across boards showed how much of this activation coverage the search had reached.

The learned editor received the current 121-bit board, its recorded circuit states, and the coverage already reached along that search path. It assigned probabilities to flipping each board position under two possible edit sizes.

The surrounding search evaluated both proposals and selected the more useful edit size. It also evaluated every possible one-bit alternative to assign credit. Circuit evaluation and coverage recording remained exact; the learned component guided the choice of edits.

What a simple baseline could reach

To judge the result, I measured coverage without training a model.

I evaluated 45 random boards—five at each fill level from 10% to 90%—plus the all-zero and all-one boards. Coverage for individual boards rose steadily with the number of one bits, from 32.98% for the empty board to 51.76% for the full board. Together, the 47 boards reached 64.45%, already close to the roughly 65% activation coverage reported for the ML run.

The known result boards reached some values that this baseline missed. The TWO NOT TOUCH board activated 469 previously unseen values at particular clocks, and the (* TWO STARS *) board activated 443.

Adding representative boards for all five messages increased the combined coverage from 64.45% to 65.22%. Finding the successful board therefore did not unlock most of the remaining coverage.

What the learned search found

In the reported run starting from random boards, the learned search reached the exact all-one input and produced BIG BANG. It did not find boards producing TWO NOT TOUCH or (* TWO STARS *).

Earlier runs had received EMPTY SKY as a starting example. TRY AGAIN was the circuit’s common fallback output, so encountering it did not show that the model had discovered a special input.

Reaching BIG BANG showed that the complete search system could follow the direction toward more one bits. The baseline helps explain why: denser boards already tended to produce higher coverage.

The experiment did not establish how much the neural model contributed. The surrounding search performed substantial selection and evaluation of alternative edits, and I had not saved a matched comparison using an untrained model or a greedy search.

It also exposed a limitation of the objective: activating more internal values did not necessarily move the search toward the successful board. The learned search explored circuit behavior, but the puzzle had already been solved by asking Z3 exactly which outputs were possible.
